source.section: Area Ratios Related to Side Length Ratios

subtopic: Area ratios with a shared angle

problem.text: In the right triangle $\triangle ACE$, we have $AC = 12$, $CE = 16$, and $EA = 20$. Points $B$, $D$, and $F$ are located on $AC$, $CE$, and $EA$, respectively, so that $AB = 3$, $CD = 4$, and $EF = 5$. What is the ratio of the area of $\triangle DBF$ to that of $\triangle ACE$?

steps.title: Where to start: subtract the three corner triangles
steps.body:
Triangle $DBF$ is awkward to measure directly, but the clue is that it leaves three corner triangles $ABF$, $BCD$ and $DEF$, and each one shares a whole angle with $\triangle ACE$. So we find each corner as a fraction of $[ACE]$ and subtract:
$$\frac{[DBF]}{[ACE]} = 1 - \frac{[ABF]}{[ACE]} - \frac{[BCD]}{[ACE]} - \frac{[DEF]}{[ACE]}.$$

your_turn.prompt: Find the other pieces of the sides: $BC$, $DE$ and $AF$.

steps.title: The shared-angle rule at $A$
steps.body: The area of a triangle is $\tfrac{1}{2}ab\sin\theta$ for two sides $a$, $b$ and the angle $\theta$ between them. Triangles $ABF$ and $ACE$ have the same angle at $A$, so the $\tfrac{1}{2}\sin A$ cancels and the area ratio is the product of the sides around $A$: $\frac{[ABF]}{[ACE]} = \frac{AB\cdot AF}{AC\cdot AE}$.

steps.title: The same rule at $C$
steps.body: Triangles $BCD$ and $ACE$ share the angle at $C$, so $\frac{[BCD]}{[ACE]} = \frac{CB\cdot CD}{CA\cdot CE}$. Careful: use the pieces that touch the angle, so the side on $AC$ is $CB = 9$, not $AB = 3$.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body:
At $E$, triangles $DEF$ and $ACE$ share the angle, so $\frac{[DEF]}{[ACE]} = \frac{ED\cdot EF}{EC\cdot EA} = \frac{12\cdot 5}{16\cdot 20} = \frac{3}{16}$ as well.
$$\frac{[DBF]}{[ACE]} = 1 - \frac{3}{16} - \frac{3}{16} - \frac{3}{16} = \frac{7}{16}$$
The answer is **(E)**.
